newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Dangers lurk as Vietnam goes from boom to boom.
newsitem.headline: Dangers lurk as Vietnam goes from boom to boom.

text.p: Vietnam looks set to continue along a path of rapid economic growth over the next two years but will have to tackle several new problems to ensure social cohesion, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.

The bank said in its annual report that the communist country, which launched an experiment in reform along market lines more than a decade ago, was likely to see gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 9.5 percent this year and 9.3 percent in 1998.
The economy grew at 9.5 percent in both 1995 and 1996 and growth has averaged 8.5 percent over the past six years.
But the ADB said there was reason for concern over the widening of the savings-investment gap, an erosion of social services and growing rural-urban disparities.
"Each of the challenges will have to be addressed with vigour if Vietnam's development is to continue without undue stress on social cohesion," it said.

The bank, which is the fourth biggest donor of foreign aid to Vietnam, said the main challenge facing the government in macroeconomic management was the country's heavy dependence on external resources to finance rising investment.

Despite a rapid increase in national savings, it has not kept pace with growth of domestic investment -- the ADB expects savings to be 19.6 percent of gross national product (GNP) and domestic investment to be 31.0 percent of GNP this year.
The report said the lag in savings growth had led to the emergence of a resource gap which was reflected in a current account deficit of more than 12 percent of GNP.
The ADB said the high level of external inflows, which finance the current account deficit, could be viewed as a measure of the international financial community's confidence in Vietnam.

"On the other hand, it is also a potential source of fragility as it implies that the sustainability of high growth is dependent on the continuation of a positive international investment climate and strong donor support for the country's reform and development programme," it said.

The Bank also warned that the country needed to improve its health and education services, which have become less effective as a result of the new focus on market forces, and also to tackle a widening wealth gap.

"...the government should develop specific growth and investment strategies that are suited to the particular circumstances of each region in order to distribute the fruits of growth more widely," it said.
